---
title: "Counts and rates: analysis of deviance with anova_count()"
description: >
  A walkthrough of anova_count() on the warpbreaks and insurance-claims data:
  Poisson or negative binomial, rate ratios, marginal rates, exposure offsets,
  groups with no events and frequency weights.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4, dpi = 96, out.width = "100%")
```

```{r libs}
library(anovakit)
```

`anova_count()` fits a regression for a count response (the number of
breaks, claims, visits or incidents) across one or more grouping variables. It
starts from a Poisson model, checks it for overdispersion, and moves to a
negative binomial model when the counts vary more than a Poisson allows. It
reports an analysis of deviance table, incidence rate ratios, estimated
marginal rates and pairwise rate ratios. With an exposure column (time at
risk, number of policies) it compares rates rather than counts.

For a yes/no outcome, use `anova_bin()` ([walkthrough](binary.html)); for
other response distributions, `anova_glm()` ([walkthrough](glm.html)).
[Choose an analysis](choosing.html) sets out the choice.

## The data

`warpbreaks` records the number of warp breaks on each of 54 looms, where a
loom corresponds to a fixed length of yarn, for two types of wool (`A`, `B`)
at three levels of tension (`L`, `M`, `H`): a 2 by 3 factorial experiment with
9 looms in each cell.

```{r data}
head(warpbreaks)
table(warpbreaks$wool, warpbreaks$tension)
aggregate(breaks ~ wool + tension, data = warpbreaks,
          FUN = function(x) round(c(mean = mean(x), variance = var(x)), 1))
```

```{r data-inline, include = FALSE}
cell_stats <- aggregate(breaks ~ wool + tension, data = warpbreaks,
                        FUN = function(x) var(x) / mean(x))
```

The breaks are counts, so a Poisson model is the natural starting point. A
Poisson distribution has its variance equal to its mean, and here the variance
within each cell is between `r round(min(cell_stats$breaks), 1)` and
`r round(max(cell_stats$breaks), 1)` times the mean. The counts are
*overdispersed*, and the function deals with that first.

## Fitting the model

Columns are named as character strings: the response, then the grouping
variables. This is a designed factorial experiment, and whether the effect of
tension depends on the wool is part of the question, so the model includes the
interaction:

```{r fit}
fit <- anova_count(warpbreaks, "breaks", c("wool", "tension"),
                   interaction = TRUE)
fit
```

Reading the printout from the top:

- The method names the model fitted: a negative binomial regression, where
  you might have expected a Poisson one.
- `Observations used: 54`, all of them.
- The omnibus table, headed with what it holds: Type II tests,
  likelihood-ratio chi-square statistics.
- The notes: why the model is negative binomial, and a warning about how far
  its tests can be trusted with 9 looms per cell. Both are discussed in the
  next section and [below](#what-the-notes-say).
- The plots that were built (they are not drawn until you ask).

`summary(fit)` prints this plus the assumption checks, the rate ratios, the
marginal means and the pairwise comparisons.

## Poisson, negative binomial or quasi-Poisson

The `model` argument decides the model. Its default, `"auto"`, fits a Poisson
model first and computes its Pearson dispersion: the sum of squared Pearson
residuals divided by the residual degrees of freedom, which is about 1 when the
Poisson variance is right. Above `overdispersion_threshold` (1.5 by default)
the function fits a negative binomial model instead, which needs the MASS
package (without it, or if that fit fails, it uses quasi-Poisson).
`$model_type` records the outcome:

```{r model-type}
fit$model_type
fit$dispersion
fit$model_dispersion
```

`$dispersion` is the Pearson dispersion of the *Poisson* fit, the statistic
the decision was made on: `r round(fit$dispersion, 2)`, well above 1.5.
`$model_dispersion` is the same statistic for the model returned. At
`r round(fit$model_dispersion, 2)` it says the negative binomial's variance
function, `mu + mu^2 / theta`, has absorbed the extra variation. The second
note gives theta, `r round(fit$model$theta, 1)`, and adds a warning: with 9
observations per cell the negative binomial's likelihood-ratio tests and Wald
intervals are markedly anti-conservative, and quasi-Poisson F tests are better
calibrated at this size.

Set `model` yourself to take the decision out of the function's hands. Here
is the interaction test under each of the three models:

```{r model-compare}
models <- c("poisson", "quasipoisson", "negbin")
fits <- lapply(models, function(m)
  anova_count(warpbreaks, "breaks", c("wool", "tension"), interaction = TRUE,
              model = m, plots = FALSE))
data.frame(model = vapply(fits, `[[`, "", "model_type"),
           test = vapply(fits, function(f) attr(f$anova, "statistic"), ""),
           statistic = vapply(fits, function(f) f$anova$statistic[3], 0),
           p_value = vapply(fits, function(f) f$anova$p_value[3], 0))
```

The Poisson model, which ignores the overdispersion, puts the p-value for the
interaction below one in a million. Both models that allow for it put it
between 0.01 and 0.05. An explicit `model = "poisson"` is kept even on data
like these, with a note:

```{r model-poisson-notes}
fits[[1]]$notes[1]
```

The note puts a size on the problem: at a dispersion of
`r round(fits[[1]]$dispersion, 2)`, a nominal 5% test on 1 degree of freedom
rejects roughly 31% of true null hypotheses, six times as often as it should.

The quasi-Poisson model keeps the Poisson estimates and scales their variance
by the estimated dispersion. It has no likelihood, so its table uses F tests:

```{r model-quasi}
fits[[2]]$anova
fits[[2]]$notes
```

`overdispersion_threshold` moves the cut-off for `model = "auto"`. It is a
fixed cut-off rather than a test, and a Poisson model kept below it still gets
the note on inflated statistics when the dispersion is beyond what chance
would produce:

```{r model-threshold}
lenient <- anova_count(warpbreaks, "breaks", c("wool", "tension"),
                       interaction = TRUE, overdispersion_threshold = 5,
                       plots = FALSE)
lenient$model_type
lenient$notes
```

The negative binomial is a full likelihood model, and with more data per group
it is usually the better choice. With groups as small as these, follow the
note and prefer quasi-Poisson for the tests. The rest of this article stays
with the automatic choice, to show what it reports.

## The omnibus test

```{r anova}
fit$anova
```

Each row is a likelihood-ratio test: `statistic` is the increase in deviance
when the term is dropped (with theta held at its estimate), referred to a
chi-square distribution on `df` degrees of freedom. Type II means each main
effect is tested after the other and without the interaction, and the
interaction after both. The `wool:tension` row says the effect of tension
depends on the wool (p = `r signif(fit$anova$p_value[3], 2)`), so the main
effects cannot be read on their own; the rate ratios and marginal means below
show the shape of the interaction.

## Effect sizes

`$effect_sizes` holds incidence rate ratios (IRRs), each a level of a factor
against its reference (first) level:

```{r effect-sizes}
print(fit$effect_sizes, digits = 3)
```

`anova_count()` has no `reference` argument. To compare against another
level, reorder the factor before fitting, for example
`w <- warpbreaks; w$tension <- relevel(w$tension, "M")`. The tension ratios
then compare L and H with M. The omnibus table is unchanged.

An IRR is the ratio of two expected counts (or two rates, with an offset): 1
means no difference, 0.5 half as many, 2 twice as many. `factor` names the
grouping variable and `comparison` says what is compared. In a model with an
interaction, a main-effect ratio holds at the reference level of the factor it
interacts with: `B vs A at tension = L` says wool B has
`r round(fit$effect_sizes$IRR[1], 2)` times the breaks of wool A *at low
tension*. The interaction rows are ratios of rate ratios.
`(B vs A) x (M vs L)` is `r round(fit$effect_sizes$IRR[4], 2)`, so the
B-to-A ratio at medium tension is `r round(fit$effect_sizes$IRR[4], 2)` times
the B-to-A ratio at low tension.

The intervals are Wald intervals on the log scale, exponentiated, and
`p_value` tests each ratio against 1. They are always computed under
treatment (reference) coding, whatever `type` or the global `contrasts`
option; `term` gives the name of the coefficient in that coding.

## Marginal means and comparisons

`$emmeans` holds the estimated marginal means on the count scale, here the
expected breaks per loom in each cell, with intervals built on the log scale
and back-transformed:

```{r emmeans}
print(fit$emmeans, digits = 3)
```

With the full interaction in the model these are the cell means of the data;
the model contributes the intervals. `$posthoc` compares every pair of cells,
as rate ratios:

```{r posthoc}
print(fit$posthoc[, c("contrast", "IRR", "conf_low", "conf_high", "p_value",
                      "p_adjusted", "adjustment")], digits = 3)
```

`IRR` is the rate of the first cell in `contrast` divided by the rate of the
second. `p_value` is unadjusted and `p_adjusted` is adjusted for all
`r nrow(fit$posthoc)` comparisons by the method in `adjustment` (Tukey by
default; `adjust` changes it). The intervals are simultaneous.

Most of those comparisons (`A L / B M`, say) answer no question anyone asked.
For the comparisons of tensions within each wool, pass `$emmeans_object` to
emmeans:

```{r posthoc-by}
emmeans::contrast(fit$emmeans_object, method = "pairwise", by = "wool")
```

With wool A, low tension gives clearly more breaks than medium or high, which
do not differ. With wool B, high tension gives fewer breaks than the other two,
less decisively.

## Rates with an exposure offset

Counts are often collected over different amounts of exposure: more
policyholders, longer follow-up, larger areas. `MASS::Insurance` gives the
number of car insurance claims in 64 groups of policyholders, by district, car
group (engine size) and driver age, together with the number of policyholders
in each group. `District` is left out below to keep the example small.

```{r ins-data}
ins <- MASS::Insurance
head(ins)
```

A group with 1,000 policyholders will have more claims than one with 100, so
the counts must be compared per policyholder. Name the exposure column in
`offset`, on its natural scale: the function takes the logarithm itself and
enters it as `offset(log(Holders))` in the model formula.

```{r ins-fit}
ins_fit <- anova_count(ins, "Claims", c("Group", "Age"), offset = "Holders")
ins_fit
print(formula(ins_fit$model), showEnv = FALSE)
```

```{r ins-inline, include = FALSE}
ins_dfr <- df.residual(ins_fit$model)
ins_p_over <- pchisq(ins_fit$dispersion * ins_dfr, ins_dfr, lower.tail = FALSE)
```

Here the Poisson model was kept: the dispersion,
`r round(ins_fit$dispersion, 2)`, is below the threshold of 1.5, and the
Pearson test cannot tell it from 1 (p = `r round(ins_p_over, 2)`). The first
note adds that with `r ins_dfr` residual degrees of freedom the test has
little power. It gives the upper confidence bound of the dispersion, how far
the tests would be inflated at that value, and the models to use if that
matters. Both factors matter:

```{r ins-es}
print(ins_fit$effect_sizes, digits = 3)
```

The rate ratios are now ratios of claims *per policyholder*: drivers aged over
35 make `r round(ins_fit$effect_sizes$IRR[6], 2)` times as many claims per
policy as drivers under 25 with the same size of car, and cars over 2 litres
`r round(ins_fit$effect_sizes$IRR[3], 2)` times as many as cars under 1 litre.
`Group` and `Age` are ordered factors; the rate ratios still compare each
level with the first, as they would for unordered factors.

The marginal means are rates at an exposure of 1, which a note records: claims
per policyholder. The unit of the exposure is the unit of the rate, so to
report claims per thousand policyholders, give the exposure in thousands:

```{r ins-rates}
ins$thousands <- ins$Holders / 1000
per_1000 <- anova_count(ins, "Claims", c("Group", "Age"),
                        offset = "thousands", plots = FALSE)
print(per_1000$emmeans, digits = 3)
grep("exposure", per_1000$notes, value = TRUE)
all.equal(per_1000$effect_sizes, ins_fit$effect_sizes)
```

The rate ratios, and everything else except the scale of the marginal means,
are unchanged. The model is additive, so the marginal rates are reported for
each factor separately, averaged over the other (the `term` column), and
`$posthoc` compares levels within each factor:

```{r ins-posthoc}
print(per_1000$posthoc[, c("term", "contrast", "IRR", "conf_low", "conf_high",
                           "p_adjusted")], digits = 3)
```

## Checking assumptions

`$assumptions` has three elements, each documented in `?anova_count`:

```{r assumptions}
fit$assumptions
```

- `poisson_dispersion` is the Pearson dispersion of the Poisson fit (the same
  number as `$dispersion`). Near 1 the Poisson variance is adequate; well
  above it, the counts are overdispersed. Below 1 they are underdispersed,
  which is rarer and makes Poisson tests conservative.
- `model_dispersion` is the same statistic for the model returned (the same
  number as `$model_dispersion`). For a negative binomial fit, a value near 1
  says the variance function fits. A value well above 1 says it does not, and
  that the source of the extra variation (a missing grouping variable,
  clustering) needs modelling.
- `cell_counts` is the number of observations in each cell of the design
  (with frequency weights it adds the number of table rows; see
  [below](#weights-and-vcov_type)). Small cells are where the asymptotic
  tests are least trustworthy, as the note on theta said.

The model also assumes independent counts and that the log rate is additive
in the terms included, which the interaction test checks for the grouping
factors. The [diagnostics guide](diagnostics.html) covers the checks across
the package.

### A group with no events

When a group has no events at all, its fitted rate is zero, the log of it is
minus infinity, and every rate ratio involving it is undefined. `glm()` still
reports convergence, with an enormous negative coefficient. To show what the
function does, here are simulated weekly incident counts at three sites; the
true rate at `east` is 0.05 a week, small but not zero, and in ten weeks it had
no incidents:

```{r zero-data}
set.seed(1)
incidents <- data.frame(
  site = factor(rep(c("north", "south", "east"), each = 10),
                levels = c("north", "south", "east")),
  events = c(rpois(10, 2), rpois(10, 4), rpois(10, 0.05))
)
tapply(incidents$events, incidents$site, sum)
zero_fit <- anova_count(incidents, "events", "site")
zero_fit
```

The notes flag the problem. The first counts the groups with fewer than 5
events in total, whose rates rest on very little information. The third names
the group with no events, says that the rate ratios involving it, its marginal
mean and the comparisons involving it are unreliable, and says what still
works. The fourth says how the interval for that rate ratio was found. The
results bear them out:

```{r zero-es}
print(zero_fit$effect_sizes, digits = 3)
print(zero_fit$posthoc[, c("contrast", "IRR", "conf_low", "conf_high",
                           "p_adjusted")], digits = 3)
```

```{r zero-inline, include = FALSE}
east_rows <- grepl("east", zero_fit$posthoc$contrast)
east_irr <- format(signif(min(zero_fit$posthoc$IRR[east_rows]), 1),
                   scientific = TRUE)
```

`east vs north` is estimated as practically zero, with a Wald p-value of
`r round(zero_fit$effect_sizes$p_value[2], 2)`: the Wald standard error is
useless here, however clear the difference. Its interval in `$effect_sizes`
is profiled and one-sided, open at 0 and bounded above at about
`r signif(zero_fit$effect_sizes$conf_high[2], 2)`; the Wald intervals of the
comparisons with `east` in `$posthoc` run from practically 0 to infinity,
around estimates of `r east_irr` and more.
The likelihood-ratio test in the omnibus table does work, and it is the number
to report for the overall comparison. For the rate ratios involving `east`,
follow the note: collapse the level with another, or use an exact method. A
robust covariance would fail here too, and `vcov_type` falls back to the
model-based one with a note:

```{r zero-robust}
grep("Robust", anova_count(incidents, "events", "site", vcov_type = "HC3",
                           plots = FALSE)$notes, value = TRUE)
```

## Plots

`fit$plots` holds two ggplot2 objects, returned rather than drawn. Use
`plot(fit, "name")` or `fit$plots$name` to get one.

```{r plot-emmeans}
plot(fit, "emmeans")
```

The `emmeans` plot shows the estimated marginal means with their intervals.
The first grouping variable goes on the x axis and the second becomes the
colour, one line per level. Lines that are not parallel show an interaction.
For wool A, low tension stands well above medium and high; for wool B, low and
medium are together and high is lowest. The low-tension line falls steeply
from A to B while the medium one rises.

```{r plot-observed}
plot(fit, "observed")
```

The `observed` plot is a box plot of the raw counts in each cell, ordered by
median and labelled with the cell's number of observations. Look for spread
that grows with the median (expected for counts, and what the negative
binomial's variance function allows for), outlying looms, and whether the
order of the medians agrees with the marginal means.

With an offset, raw counts would mostly show where the exposure is, so the
plot shows observed rates instead: each row's count divided by its exposure,
here claims per policyholder.

```{r plot-observed-ins, fig.height = 5}
plot(ins_fit, "observed")
```

The title and the y axis name the rate. The order of the boxes follows the
rate ratios: the lowest median is for drivers over 35 with the smallest cars
(`<1l : >35`), the highest for drivers under 25 with the largest
(`>2l : <25`). A rate computed from a small exposure is noisy. The widest box,
`>2l : <25`, comes from the four groups of young drivers of large cars, which
hold between `r min(ins$Holders[ins$Group == ">2l" & ins$Age == "<25"])` and
`r max(ins$Holders[ins$Group == ">2l" & ins$Age == "<25"])` policyholders each.

The plot should tell the same story as the marginal rates. To check, pool the
claims and policyholders by age band:

```{r plot-observed-check}
by_age <- aggregate(cbind(Claims, Holders) ~ Age, data = ins, FUN = sum)
by_age$rate <- by_age$Claims / by_age$Holders
by_age
ins_fit$emmeans[ins_fit$emmeans$term == "Age", c("Age", "estimate")]
```

The pooled rates fall with age, as the marginal rates do. The numbers differ
because the marginal rates are adjusted for car group and average over the
four car groups equally, while the pooled rates are weighted by where the
policyholders are. Each plot is a ggplot and can be modified with `+`;
[Plots and themes](visuals.html) has more.

## Options

### `interaction`

The model is additive by default. An additive model gives each factor's
effect averaged over the other, which is what you want when the interaction is
absent and misleading when it is present. The additive fit of the same data
reports marginal means for each factor separately:

```{r additive}
additive <- anova_count(warpbreaks, "breaks", c("wool", "tension"),
                        plots = FALSE)
additive$anova
print(additive$emmeans, digits = 3)
```

The wool rows average over tensions, so they hide the fact that the wool
difference runs in opposite directions at low and medium tension. Decide on
the interaction before looking at the answers, as the design here justified.

### `test_statistic`

`"LR"` (the default) gives likelihood-ratio tests; `"Wald"` gives Wald
chi-square tests; `"F"` gives F tests, which a quasi-Poisson model uses
anyway. On a negative binomial (or Poisson) model, `"F"` estimates a
dispersion from the Pearson residuals and divides the deviances by it. The
table then becomes a quasi-likelihood test while the rate ratios still assume
the model's own dispersion, and the note says so:

```{r test-statistic}
wald_fit <- anova_count(warpbreaks, "breaks", c("wool", "tension"),
                        interaction = TRUE, test_statistic = "Wald",
                        plots = FALSE)
wald_fit$anova
f_fit <- anova_count(warpbreaks, "breaks", c("wool", "tension"),
                     interaction = TRUE, test_statistic = "F", plots = FALSE)
f_fit$anova
grep("test_statistic", f_fit$notes, value = TRUE)
```

For quasi-likelihood inference throughout, use `model = "quasipoisson"`.

### Weights and `vcov_type`

`weights` names a column of prior weights. Whole-number weights, some above
1, are frequency weights: each row stands for that many identical
observations, and the analysis is the one the expanded data would give.
`InsectSprays` has 12 insect counts for each of six sprays; as a frequency
table it has one row per spray and count, with the number of times that count
occurred in `Freq`:

```{r weights-table}
spray_tab <- as.data.frame(table(spray = InsectSprays$spray,
                                 count = InsectSprays$count),
                           stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
spray_tab <- spray_tab[spray_tab$Freq > 0, ]
spray_tab$count <- as.numeric(spray_tab$count)
head(spray_tab)
c(rows = nrow(spray_tab), observations = sum(spray_tab$Freq))
```

Fitted to the original rows and to the table, the analysis is the same:

```{r weights-fit}
from_rows <- anova_count(InsectSprays, "count", "spray", plots = FALSE)
from_table <- anova_count(spray_tab, "count", "spray", weights = "Freq",
                          plots = FALSE)
c(rows = from_rows$dispersion, table = from_table$dispersion)
all.equal(from_rows$anova, from_table$anova)
all.equal(from_rows$effect_sizes, from_table$effect_sizes)
grep("frequency weights", from_table$notes, value = TRUE)
```

```{r weights-inline, include = FALSE}
pois_table <- glm(count ~ spray, family = poisson, data = spray_tab,
                  weights = Freq)
row_disp <- sum(residuals(pois_table, type = "pearson")^2) /
  df.residual(pois_table)
```

Three things are specific to `anova_count()`. First, the dispersion that
decides between Poisson and negative binomial divides by the
`r sum(spray_tab$Freq)` observations the weights represent minus the
parameters, not by the `r nrow(spray_tab)` rows. Dividing by rows, as
`glm()`'s own residual degrees of freedom would, gives
`r round(row_disp, 2)` instead of `r round(from_rows$dispersion, 2)`, and
could switch a Poisson model to a negative binomial one for no reason. Here
both values are above the threshold of 1.5, so the choice is the same either
way; the correct value is only just above it, and the theta note says the
negative binomial has only weakly overdispersed data to work with.

Second, `$assumptions$cell_counts` gives two sizes: `n` is the number of
observations in each cell (the sum of the weights) and `rows` the number of
table rows behind them.

```{r weights-cells}
from_table$assumptions$cell_counts
```

Third, the `observed` plot is built from the expanded table (one row per
observation), so its boxes match the plot of the `r nrow(InsectSprays)`
original rows. A table that stands for more than 200,000 observations is not
expanded: the boxes are then built from one row per table row, and a note
says so.

Weights that are not whole numbers are not frequencies. They are used as
given, so their scale matters, and the dispersion that chooses the model is
computed with them rescaled to average 1. `vcov_type` (`"HC0"` to `"HC4"`)
gives heteroscedasticity-consistent (sandwich) standard errors for the rate
ratios, the marginal means and the comparisons, and for the omnibus table only
with `test_statistic = "Wald"`. With frequency weights they are computed as on
the expanded data. [Weights and robust standard errors](weights.html) has an
example on `warpbreaks`, the rules for every kind of weight, and the cases
where the model-based covariance is used instead, such as a group with no
events ([above](#a-group-with-no-events)).

### `type`, `adjust`, `conf_level` and `posthoc`

`type = "III"` fits the model under sum-to-zero contrasts, which changes the
main-effect rows of `$anova` when there is an interaction; the rate ratios are
unchanged. `posthoc = FALSE` skips the pairwise comparisons, with a note:

```{r type3}
type3 <- anova_count(warpbreaks, "breaks", c("wool", "tension"),
                     interaction = TRUE, type = "III", posthoc = FALSE,
                     plots = FALSE)
type3$anova
all.equal(type3$effect_sizes, fit$effect_sizes)
grep("posthoc|still reports", type3$notes, value = TRUE)
```

`adjust` sets the multiplicity adjustment for `$posthoc` and `conf_level` the
level of every interval, as in the other model-based functions; the
[binary-outcomes walkthrough](binary.html) shows both.

## What the notes say

```{r notes}
fit$notes
```

- The first note records the model choice: the Poisson dispersion, the
  threshold, and the model fitted instead. It also says how to override it.
- The second gives the negative binomial's theta, the variance function it
  implies, and how far to trust the tests and intervals given the size of the
  smallest group. With 9 looms per cell it recommends quasi-Poisson F tests.
  In a write-up of these data, report that version of the interaction test
  alongside (or instead of) this one.

There is no note on the layout of the marginal means, because with the
interaction in the model they are cells; an additive fit (the insurance model,
for one) adds a note explaining the per-factor layout. Other fits in this
article showed the notes on an explicit Poisson model with overdispersion, on
quasi-Poisson F tests, on a kept Poisson model whose dispersion test has
little power, on exposure, on sparse and empty groups, on robust standard
errors, and on frequency weights. [Working with results](results.html)
explains how `$notes` fits with the rest of the object.

## Reporting the result

```{r report-inline, include = FALSE}
a <- fit$anova
qp <- fits[[2]]$anova
es <- fit$effect_sizes
fmt_p <- function(p) {
  if (p < 0.001) "< 0.001" else paste("=", sprintf("%.3f", p))
}
```

A write-up might read:

> Warp breaks were analysed with a negative binomial regression on wool,
> tension and their interaction (Pearson dispersion of the Poisson model
> `r sprintf("%.2f", fit$dispersion)`; theta =
> `r sprintf("%.1f", fit$model$theta)`).
> The effect of tension depended on the wool (likelihood-ratio
> χ²(`r a$df[3]`) = `r sprintf("%.2f", a$statistic[3])`, p
> `r fmt_p(a$p_value[3])`; quasi-Poisson F(`r qp$df[3]`, `r qp$df[4]`) =
> `r sprintf("%.2f", qp$statistic[3])`, p `r fmt_p(qp$p_value[3])`). At low
> tension wool B produced fewer breaks than wool A (rate ratio
> `r sprintf("%.2f", es$IRR[1])`, 95% CI `r sprintf("%.2f", es$conf_low[1])`
> to `r sprintf("%.2f", es$conf_high[1])`), and with wool A both medium and
> high tension reduced breaks by about half relative to low tension (rate
> ratios `r sprintf("%.2f", es$IRR[2])` and `r sprintf("%.2f", es$IRR[3])`).
